Gapless Nature of Spin Liquid in the S=1/2S=1/2 Kagome Heisenberg
Antiferromagnet with Neural-Network Quantum States

Andreas Raikos Email: andreas.raikos@irsamc.ups-tlse.fr Affiliation: Université de Toulouse, CNRS, Laboratoire de Physique Théorique, Toulouse, France.    Alessandro Sinibaldi Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland    Riccardo Rende Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10010    Giuseppe Carleo Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland    Federico Becca Email: fbecca@units.it Affiliation: Dipartimento di Fisica, Università di Trieste, Strada Costiera 11, I-34151 Trieste, Italy    Luciano Loris Viteritti Email: luciano.viteritti@epfl.ch Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland
November 13, 2026
Abstract

Whether the spin-1/21/2 kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet hosts a gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} or a gapless U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid remains a central open question in frustrated magnetism. Here, we address this question by directly computing the triplet gap with a neural-network quantum state that does not presuppose any specific spin-liquid structure. Applying a time-reversal symmetric transformer-based ansatz to clusters of up to 768768 sites, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies on two-dimensional lattices with periodic boundary conditions and estimate an energy per site of −0.43873​(12)-0.43873(12) in the thermodynamic limit. Finite-size scaling of the magnetic order parameter and triplet excitation gap shows that both extrapolate to zero in the thermodynamic limit. Together, these results provide independent and direct evidence of a gapless spin-liquid ground state, consistent with the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid. More broadly, they demonstrate that neural-network quantum states can resolve ground-state properties of frustrated quantum magnets that remain challenging for conventional numerical methods.

Introduction.

The S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the kagome lattice

H^=J​∑⟨i,j⟩𝑺^i⋅𝑺^j\hat{H}=J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{j} (1)

represents a paradigm for the geometric frustration and a prototypical candidate for hosting a quantum spin liquid ground state [72, 30, 71]. Here, J>0J>0 is the antiferromagnetic super-exchange and ⟨i,j⟩\langle i,j\rangle denotes nearest-neighbor pairs on the kagome lattice. The interest in this model was raised following the discovery of several materials featuring localized S=1/2S=1/2 moments that interact via super-exchange within quasi-two-dimensional kagome layers. The most notable example is given by the so-called Herbertsmithite ZnCu3(OH)6Cl2 in which copper ions host S=1/2S=1/2 moments forming kagome layers [35, 19, 9]. Inelastic neutron scattering has revealed a broad continuum of spin excitations [17], but the nature of its low-energy spectrum remains debated. Neutron magnetic resonance (NMR) and neutron scattering measurements have supported a finite spin gap [13], whereas later NMR studies found evidence for gapless excitations [27]. Related kagome compounds have also shown signatures consistent with gapless excitations with conical (Dirac) dispersion [12, 73].

Despite the deceptively simple form of the Hamiltonian in Eq. 1, characterizing its ground state remains a formidable challenge. Exact diagonalizations reveal a dense low-energy spectrum [53, 29], which represents one of the most intriguing aspects of quantum magnets [37]. Series expansions and entanglement-renormalization calculations favored a valence-bond crystal with a 36-site unit cell [54, 11]. Subsequent density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations found evidence in favor of a gapped spin liquid [71, 10], further characterized by the presence of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} topological order [25]. Alternatively, variational wave functions, constructed by Gutzwiller-projected Abrikosov fermions, suggested the possibility that the spin liquid is gapless, with Dirac points in the spinon dispersion and emerging U⁡(1)U(1) gauge excitations [42, 22, 23]. Further support in favor of the existence of gapless excitations was given by tensor-network states, either by pushing the bond dimension to large values (working with projected-entangled pair states) [31] or by imposing a flux insertion to modify the boundary conditions (within the DMRG approach) [18]. The dynamical structure factor was also evaluated using DMRG, revealing a low-energy continuum of excitations that is consistent with findings from inelastic neutron scattering [75]. Other candidate ground states have also been proposed, including a recent claim of a spinon pair density wave [76], which, however, has been challenged due to issues with the underlying Monte Carlo sampling [26]. Still, a direct computation of the spin gap (e.g., for Δ​S=1\Delta S=1 excitations) remained out of reach for large-scale, high-precision numerical methods. Progress in this direction requires controlling both the variational approximation and the approach to the two-dimensional thermodynamic limit. In this respect, neural-network quantum states (NQS) [5] offer a unique way to reach very high accuracy [7, 45] on large clusters [67], since their representational power can be systematically improved, and the variational state can be optimized directly on two-dimensional lattices with fully periodic boundary conditions. In addition, the implementation of lattice and spin symmetries improves the variational accuracy and enables a direct control of quantum numbers [38, 39, 43, 66], so that low-lying excited states can be targeted as the lowest-energy states in different symmetry sectors.

In this Letter, we employ a time-reversal symmetric transformer-based NQS [64, 66], optimized within the variational Monte Carlo (VMC) framework [2], to study the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet of Eq. 1 on fully periodic L×LL\times L clusters with N=3​L2N=3L^{2} spins, up to N=768N=768. For all clusters with L≥6L\geq 6, we obtain the lowest variational energies reported to date, and the variational accuracy remains approximately constant with system size, as required for a meaningful finite-size scaling. The magnetic order parameter extrapolates to zero in the thermodynamic limit. Our central result is that the triplet gap, computed directly on large clusters, decreases systematically with system size and extrapolates to zero within error bars in the thermodynamic limit.

Since the transformer ansatz does not presuppose any specific spin-liquid structure, these results provide strong numerical evidence for a gapless spin-liquid ground state consistent with the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac state [42, 22, 23].

Methods.

NQS are variational ansätze in which a neural network parametrizes the amplitudes of a quantum many-body wave function, providing a compact representation to approximate the ground state or low-lying excited states in an exponentially large Hilbert space [49, 28, 34, 21]. To study the Hamiltonian in Eq. 1, we employ an NQS based on the Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture [64, 66], augmented with the spatial attention mechanism [67]. This architecture has been successfully applied to a broad range of strongly correlated spin systems [66, 67, 55, 65, 7, 50, 41, 33, 44, 46]. In general, the ViT maps a spin configuration 𝝈=(σ1,…,σN)\boldsymbol{\sigma}=(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{N}), with σi=±1\sigma_{i}=\pm 1, to the complex-valued amplitude Ψθ​(𝝈)\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) in three steps, where θ\theta denotes the variational parameters. First, the configuration is partitioned into patches, each of which is embedded into a vector in a dd-dimensional feature space. For the kagome lattice, we choose each patch to contain the three spins of one of the L2L^{2} kagome primitive unit cells, so that the input to the transformer is the sequence (𝒙1,𝒙2,…,𝒙L2)(\boldsymbol{x}_{1},\boldsymbol{x}_{2},\ldots,\boldsymbol{x}_{L^{2}}) with 𝒙i∈ℝd\boldsymbol{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Second, this sequence is processed by nln_{l} transformer encoder layers with spatial attention mechanism [67]. Third, the output of the last layer is sum-pooled over the patch index and mapped by a complex-valued nonlinear layer to the amplitude Ψθ​(𝝈)∈ℂ\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})\in\mathbb{C}. Further details on each component of the architecture can be found in Ref. [66].

Here, we introduce a simple modification of this architecture that exploits the fact that the Hamiltonian in Eq. 1 is time-reversal symmetric. Its eigenstates can therefore be chosen real, a property not explicitly imposed by the standard complex-valued ansatz. We enforce this condition directly at the network output by defining the symmetrized wave function

ΨθTR​(𝝈)=Ψθ​(𝝈)+Ψθ∗​(𝝈),\Psi^{\text{TR}}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})+\Psi^{*}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})\,, (2)

which is real by construction and requires neither additional parameters nor additional network evaluations. This projection both accelerates optimization and improves variational accuracy (see End Matter). The complex-valued output layer still encodes the phase structure through the representations learned by the transformer [66], while phase deviations from 00 and π\pi, which a complex-valued ansatz must suppress during optimization [60, 63], are removed by construction. The resulting architecture is illustrated in Fig. 1.

The use of patches matching the unit cell, together with translation-equivariant attention and sum pooling over patches, ensures that the ViT amplitude is invariant under Bravais lattice translations of the input spin configuration, with the variational state thus belonging to the zero-momentum (Γ\Gamma) sector. Point-group and spin-inversion symmetries are instead imposed on the network output through quantum-number projection [66, 38], which improves the variational accuracy and fixes the symmetry sector of the variational state. For the ground state, we select the even spin-inversion sector (P=+1P=+1) and the A1A_{1} irreducible representation of C6​vC_{6v}. For the excited state used to compute the triplet gap (see below), we select the odd sector (P=−1P=-1) and the A2A_{2} representation for L≥6L\geq 6 (E2E_{2} for L=4L=4). Details on the optimization of the ansatz, including the choice of the irreducible representations, are reported in the Supplemental Material.

Results.

We first compare our variational ground-state energies with previous numerical results, restricting the comparison to calculations performed on finite clusters for consistency, see Fig. 2. On the smallest cluster, L=4L=4 (N=48N=48), where exact diagonalizations are available [29], our relative energy error is about 10−310^{-3} (see End Matter for additional calculations), comparable to that of DMRG on the same torus with 19 86019\,860 kept states [1]. Beyond this size, however, DMRG becomes increasingly demanding: maintaining a fixed accuracy in two dimensions generally requires the number of kept states (equivalently, the bond dimension) to grow exponentially with the system width, and fully periodic-boundary conditions impose an additional entanglement cost [58]. Consequently, on the L=6L=6 cluster, DMRG with 6 0006\,000 kept states [24] already yields a substantially higher energy than ours. On the larger clusters, our energies are also lower than those of the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid improved by one Lanczos step and by two Lanczos steps plus fixed node [22, 23]. Table 1 in the End Matter lists all our energies and variances per site, together with the V-score [69], a measure of variational accuracy. The V-score remains approximately constant with increasing LL, indicating a size-consistent variational accuracy. Overall, our energies for L≥6L\geq 6 are, to our knowledge, the lowest variational energies obtained on finite tori. The lower energies reported for the N=108N=108 torus in Ref. [76] may not constitute reliable variational estimates, as a recent work attributes them to nonergodic sampling [26].

We emphasize that, for every size studied, our energies already lie below the upper bound on the infinite-system energy obtained with DMRG [71], shown as horizontal line in Fig. 2. To estimate the ground-state energy in the thermodynamic limit, we perform zero-variance extrapolations at fixed system size (see End Matter). As shown in the inset of Fig. 2, the resulting estimates exhibit only a weak size dependence and lie below the corresponding zero-variance estimates for the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac state (improved by Lanczos steps) [22]. A constant fit of these estimates yields −0.43873​(12)-0.43873(12), compatible within the error bar with the DMRG estimate −0.4386​(5)-0.4386(5) obtained by extrapolating S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetric calculations on long cylinders [10].

We next examine the spin-spin correlations in the ground state. For an exactly S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetric singlet, the correlations are identical for all three spin components; since our ansatz fixes only StotzS^{z}_{\mathrm{tot}} and does not enforce the full S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry, longitudinal and transverse correlations can differ at finite variational accuracy. In the following, we restrict our analysis to the longitudinal (z​zzz) correlations rather than the transverse (or isotropic) ones. Indeed, the latter ones exhibit a strong dependence on the accuracy of the wave function (as measured by its energy variance), converging toward the longitudinal values only as the accuracy improves; by contrast, the longitudinal correlations remain largely insensitive when improving the accuracy (see End Matter).

We therefore evaluate the spin structure factor as S⁡(𝒒)=3N​∑i,jei​𝒒⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j)​⟨S^iz​S^jz⟩S(\boldsymbol{q})=\frac{3}{N}\sum_{i,j}e^{\mathrm{i}\boldsymbol{q}\cdot(\boldsymbol{r}_{i}-\boldsymbol{r}_{j})}\langle\hat{S}^{z}_{i}\hat{S}^{z}_{j}\rangle. Fig. 3 shows S⁡(𝒒)S(\boldsymbol{q}) on the L=16L=16 cluster, with maxima at the six symmetry-related MM points of the extended Brillouin zone. To assess whether these peaks signal magnetic long-range order or not, we study the square magnetic order parameter m2=Speak/Nm^{2}=S_{\mathrm{peak}}/N, where Speak=13​[S⁡(M1)+S⁡(M2)+S⁡(M3)]S_{\mathrm{peak}}=\frac{1}{3}[S(M_{1})+S(M_{2})+S(M_{3})], with M1M_{1}, M2M_{2}, and M3M_{3} denoting the three inequivalent, symmetry-related MM points (see Fig. 3). In Fig. 4, we report m2m^{2} as a function of 1/L1/L. The approximately linear behavior of these data on log-log axes (shown in the inset) suggests an algebraic decay of m2m^{2} with the system size. A fit of the form m2∝L−αm^{2}\propto L^{-\alpha} yields an effective exponent α≈2.01​(1)\alpha\approx 2.01(1), consistent with m2m^{2} vanishing in the thermodynamic limit. This implies an approximately constant peak of the structure factor Speak∝L2−α≈constS_{\mathrm{peak}}\propto L^{2-\alpha}\approx\text{const}. Remarkably, this scaling closely matches that of the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid, shown in the same panel as comparison, indicating that our results are compatible with such a gapless state.

To probe the excitation spectrum more directly, we compute the triplet gap Δ\Delta, which is the difference of the total variational energies of the lowest singlet and triplet states. We target these two states by optimizing wave functions projected onto even (P=+1P=+1) and odd (P=−1P=-1) spin-inversion parity, respectively. In both cases, we consider Stotz=0S^{z}_{\mathrm{tot}}=0 and the zero momentum sector, while different point-group symmetries are considered, see Supplemental Material. The parity projection separates even and odd total spins: the two states are orthogonal and share no total-spin sector, even though each may still mix several spin sectors of the same parity.

A common alternative is to approximate the lowest singlet and triplet by optimizing at Stotz=0S_{\mathrm{tot}}^{z}=0 and Stotz=1S_{\mathrm{tot}}^{z}=1, respectively [18, 66]. However, fixing the magnetization alone does not exclude triplet components from the Stotz=0S_{\mathrm{tot}}^{z}=0 state and, therefore, the optimization with Stotz=0S_{\mathrm{tot}}^{z}=0 may contain a contribution from the triplet, thus strongly underestimating the triplet gap. This risk is particularly severe on the kagome lattice, where exact diagonalization studies reveal an unusually dense low-energy spectrum in each total-spin sector [53, 29].

The odd-parity energies are reported in Table 2 in the End Matter, together with their variances and V-scores [69]. Because Δ\Delta is the difference of two variational energies, its accuracy depends on how evenly the two states are approximated. We quantify this balance through the ratio Vodd/VevenV_{\mathrm{odd}}/V_{\mathrm{even}} of the V-scores of the two states, shown in the inset of Fig. 5. Since the V-score is approximately proportional to the relative energy error [69], a ratio above one indicates that the triplet is described less accurately than the singlet, so that Δ\Delta is overestimated. This is the case at L=4L=4, where we obtain Δ=0.21249​(33)\Delta=0.21249(33), compared with the exact value ΔED=0.17505\Delta_{\mathrm{ED}}=0.17505 [29]. There, the V-score ratio is approximately 2.32.3, consistent with the ratio of the relative errors with respect to exact diagonalization, and this imbalance accounts for the overestimate (see also End Matter). For L≥6L\geq 6, the ratio is much closer to one, so we expect the errors of the two energies largely cancel in Δ\Delta.

As shown in the main panel of Fig. 5, the gap decreases systematically with system size, reaching Δ=0.0470​(16)\Delta=0.0470(16) for L=12L=12 (N=432N=432). Given the balanced accuracy at these sizes, this decrease is not an artifact of unevenly approximated states. We also report DMRG results for L=4,6L=4,6 tori as comparison [10]. Already at L=12L=12, our gap is approximately three times smaller than the thermodynamic-limit estimate Δ=0.13​(1)\Delta=0.13(1) obtained by extrapolating S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetric DMRG calculations on long cylinders [10]. A linear extrapolation in 1/L1/L yields Δ=−0.031​(35)\Delta=-0.031(35), consistent with a vanishing gap in the thermodynamic limit. Together with the scaling of the magnetic order parameter, which closely follows that of the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid, our result provides direct evidence for a gapless spin liquid, in agreement with Refs. [22, 23, 31] and in contrast with the gapped spin liquid proposed in Refs. [24, 10].

Conclusions.

We have studied the spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the kagome lattice using a time-reversal-symmetric transformer-based NQS on fully periodic tori containing up to N=768N=768 spins. Our calculations yield state-of-the-art variational energies, while the approximately size-independent V-score [69] indicates comparable variational accuracy across the system sizes studied. The square magnetic order parameter decreases as a power law, vanishing in the thermodynamic limit with a scaling closely matching that of the U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid [22]. By optimizing states in distinct symmetry sectors, we also obtain triplet-gap estimates on clusters containing up to N=432N=432 spins. The estimated triplet gap decreases systematically with system size and extrapolates to Δ=−0.031​(35)\Delta=-0.031(35) consistent with a vanishing gap. Together, our results provide numerical evidence for a magnetically disordered ground state with gapless excitations, compatible with a U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid.

Our work demonstrates that NQS can characterize both ground-state correlations and low-energy excitations in challenging two-dimensional frustrated magnets. Several directions merit further investigation. Alternative methods for capturing excitations that do not require imposing symmetries, such as grassmamian VMC [40, 20] and penalty-based approaches [52, 14], are worth exploring. Recent advances in fermionic neural-network wave functions [16, 51, 47, 6] also motivate extending this approach to the kagome Hubbard model. More broadly, experimental observations of spin-orbit polarons [70, 8] and of charge order intertwined with superconductivity in kagome metals [36] make correlated fermionic models on the kagome lattice a compelling target for future studies.

Code Availability.

The numerical simulations have been performed using the software libraries NetKet [4, 61] and tachys [48]. A step-by-step tutorial on the implementation of the ViT wave function in tachys is available online [62]. The code used to perform the simulations is available at https://github.com/tachys-dev/kagome_vit.

Note Added.

During the preparation of this work, two preprints appeared on arXiv investigating the same model using convolutional neural-network quantum states [59] and infinite projected entangled-pair states (iPEPS), respectively [74]. Both studies report evidence for a gapless spin-liquid ground state, consistent with our conclusions.

End Matter

Time Reversal Symmetry.

The Heisenberg Hamiltonian in Eq. 1 is time reversal symmetric, which allows us to choose its eigenstates to be real. We exploit this property by defining the output of the neural network in the projected form in Eq. 2. In addition, before taking the real part in the time-reversal symmetrization, we multiply the ViT output by a fixed phase factor [3], Ψθ​(𝝈)→ei​Φ0​(𝝈)​Ψθ​(𝝈)\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})\rightarrow e^{i\Phi_{0}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})}\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}). Here Φ0(𝝈)=−12∑iϕiσi\Phi_{0}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\phi_{i}\sigma_{i} is the phase of the classical coplanar 𝒒=𝟎\boldsymbol{q}=\boldsymbol{0} state and ϕi∈{0,2π/3,−2π/3}\phi_{i}\in\{0,2\pi/3,-2\pi/3\} is the angle of the spin at site ii, which is the same on all sites of a given sublattice. This phase factor is introduced to accelerate convergence and does not restrict the variational state, since the network can freely modify the sign structure through the phase of Ψθ​(𝝈)\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}). We have verified that optimizations without it eventually converge to the same results.

Using real amplitudes offers two main advantages. First, the logarithmic derivatives with respect to the variational parameters are also real. This halves the dimension of the sample-space linear system solved by Stochastic Reconfiguration (SR) [56, 57]-based methods to compute the parameter update [7, 45], yielding an empirical three- to four speedup per optimization step.

Second, it improves the variational accuracy achieved in practice. To illustrate this, Fig. 6 compares the optimization of the same architecture with and without the time-reversal-symmetric output layer defined in Eq. 2, on the L=4L=4 cluster (N=48N=48). The real-output network converges to a lower variational energy while requiring approximately one-third of the time per optimization step.

Numerical Values of Energies and Variances.

Table 1 and Table 2 report the final energy per site, variance per site, and V-score after point-group restoration for states with even (up to L=14L=14) and odd spin-inversion parity, respectively. At L=16L=16, we report the values before the point-group projection, since the cost of becomes considerable at this size. The corresponding V-scores are denoted by VevenV_{\text{even}} and VoddV_{\text{odd}}. All quantities are estimated from approximately 10610^{6} Monte Carlo samples per state, generated using blurred sampling [68] to obtain an unbiased estimate of the energy variance.

Variance Extrapolations.

In Figure 7, we show how an extrapolation in the energy variance improves upon the variational energies of Table 1. For each system size we consider transformers with nl=4n_{l}=4, 66 and 88 layers (before the point-group projection) and plot their energy per site against the variance per site. A linear fit is extrapolated to zero variance, and the uncertainty of the extrapolated energy is estimated by repeating the fit on Gaussian-distributed replicas of the data within their error bars. For L=4L=4 we obtain −0.43865​(16)-0.43865(16), consistent with the exact value −0.438704-0.438704, whereas the S​U​(2)SU(2) DMRG energy reported in Ref. [10] for the same torus, −0.4383​(2)-0.4383(2), lies two error bars above it. For L=6L=6 the extrapolation gives −0.43947​(43)-0.43947(43), while the S​U​(2)SU(2) DMRG energy of the same torus is −0.4383​(3)-0.4383(3) [10]. The extrapolated energies for L=10L=10 and 1414 are −0.43837​(29)-0.43837(29), and −0.43903​(44)-0.43903(44), respectively.

S​U​(2)SU(2) extrapolations of the structure factor.

Here, we detail the calculation of the spin structure factor, providing evidence that the z​zzz component yields the best approximation to the full isotropic value. We compare three estimators of the square magnetic order parameter, which differ in the spin components entering the peak of the structure factor: the isotropic estimator miso2m^{2}_{\text{iso}}, obtained from Siso​(𝒒)=1N​∑i,jei​𝒒⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j)​⟨𝑺^i⋅𝑺^j⟩S_{\text{iso}}(\boldsymbol{q})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i,j}e^{\mathrm{i}\boldsymbol{q}\cdot(\boldsymbol{r}_{i}-\boldsymbol{r}_{j})}\langle\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{j}\rangle; the transverse estimator m⟂2m^{2}_{\perp}, obtained from S⟂​(𝒒)=32​N​∑i,jei​𝒒⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j)​⟨S^ix​S^jx+S^iy​S^jy⟩S_{\perp}(\boldsymbol{q})=\frac{3}{2N}\sum_{i,j}e^{\mathrm{i}\boldsymbol{q}\cdot(\boldsymbol{r}_{i}-\boldsymbol{r}_{j})}\langle\hat{S}^{x}_{i}\hat{S}^{x}_{j}+\hat{S}^{y}_{i}\hat{S}^{y}_{j}\rangle; and the longitudinal estimator m2m^{2} used in the main text, obtained from the z​zzz structure factor S⁡(𝒒)=3N​∑i,jei​𝒒⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j)​⟨S^iz​S^jz⟩S(\boldsymbol{q})=\frac{3}{N}\sum_{i,j}e^{\mathrm{i}\boldsymbol{q}\cdot(\boldsymbol{r}_{i}-\boldsymbol{r}_{j})}\langle\hat{S}^{z}_{i}\hat{S}^{z}_{j}\rangle. The constant prefactors are chosen such that the three estimators coincide for an exactly S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetric state. Figure 8 shows the three estimators for three variational states of increasing accuracy, obtained with transformers of different depths, as a function of the energy variance per site, which we take as a measure of variational accuracy. For each estimator, we fit the data and extrapolate to zero variance. At the finite accuracy reached here, m2m^{2} is already converged with respect to the variance, whereas m⟂2m^{2}_{\perp} and miso2m^{2}_{\text{iso}} are overestimated and decrease systematically toward it as the variance is reduced. Accordingly, the extrapolations to zero variance, where S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry is restored, yield values consistent with m2m^{2} and well below the finite-variance estimates of m⟂2m^{2}_{\perp} and miso2m^{2}_{\text{iso}}. The inset shows that the deviation of m⟂2m^{2}_{\perp} and miso2m^{2}_{\text{iso}} from m2m^{2} decreases together with ⟨S^2⟩/N\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle/N, confirming that it originates from the residual S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetry breaking of the variational state and is progressively suppressed as the variational accuracy improves. These results justify using m2m^{2} as our estimator of the magnetic order parameter.

“Gapless Nature of Spin Liquid in the S=1/2S=1/2 Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet with Neural-Network Quantum States”

Optimization Details

To target the lowest singlet and the lowest triplet within the zero-momentum sector, we project the wave function onto even and odd spin-inversion parity, respectively, using the symmetrized variational states Ψθ±​(𝝈)=ΨθTR​(𝝈)±ΨθTR​(−𝝈)\Psi^{\pm}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=\Psi^{\mathrm{TR}}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})\pm\Psi^{\mathrm{TR}}_{\theta}(-\boldsymbol{\sigma}), where −𝝈-\boldsymbol{\sigma} denotes the configuration with all spins flipped. The variational parameters θ\theta are optimized within the variational Monte Carlo (VMC) framework [2] by minimizing the variational energy Eθ±=⟨Ψθ±|H^|Ψθ±⟩/⟨Ψθ±|Ψθ±⟩E^{\pm}_{\theta}=\langle\Psi^{\pm}_{\theta}|\hat{H}|\Psi^{\pm}_{\theta}\rangle/\langle\Psi^{\pm}_{\theta}|\Psi^{\pm}_{\theta}\rangle, which is estimated via Markov chain Monte Carlo from configurations sampled according to the Born distribution Pθ±​(𝝈)∝|Ψθ±​(𝝈)|2P^{\pm}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})\propto|\Psi^{\pm}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})|^{2}. All optimizations are performed in the Sz=0S^{z}=0 sector, which is enforced by the transition rule of the Monte Carlo sampling. The energy is minimized with the MARCH optimizer [16], which builds on SR [56, 57] in the formulation suited to a number of variational parameters much larger than the number of samples [7, 45, 15]. We use MARCH parameters μ=0.95\mu=0.95 and β=0.995\beta=0.995, a diagonal shift of 10−410^{-4}, and M=214M=2^{14} Monte Carlo samples. Unless stated otherwise, all optimizations use a transformer with nl=8n_{l}=8 layers, h=12h=12 attention heads, and embedding dimension d=72d=72.

First, we perform an initial optimization of 10410^{4} steps with a learning rate decaying from 5×10−35\times 10^{-3} to 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} following a cosine schedule [32]. We then restore the C6​vC_{6v} point-group symmetry by projection. In the following, we denote with |ΨP⟩|\Psi_{P}\rangle the optimized spin-inversion-symmetrized state of either even or odd parity. To select the irreducible representation (irrep) λ\lambda, we compute the weights wλ=⟨ΨP|P^λ|ΨP⟩/⟨ΨP|ΨP⟩w_{\lambda}=\langle\Psi_{P}|\hat{P}_{\lambda}|\Psi_{P}\rangle/\langle\Psi_{P}|\Psi_{P}\rangle in all irreps of C6​vC_{6v}, where P^λ\hat{P}_{\lambda} is the projector onto λ\lambda and ∑λwλ=1\sum_{\lambda}w_{\lambda}=1, and project onto the irrep with the largest weight. For all even states, the largest weight is in A1A_{1}, with wA1w_{A_{1}} close to one, whereas for the odd states it is in A2A_{2} for L≥6L\geq 6 and in E2E_{2} for L=4L=4. The point-group-projected state in irrep λ\lambda is Ψλ​(𝝈)=∑g∈C6​vχλ​(g)​ΨP​(g​𝝈)\Psi_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=\sum_{g\in C_{6v}}\chi_{\lambda}(g)\,\Psi_{P}(g\boldsymbol{\sigma}), where χλ​(g)\chi_{\lambda}(g) is the character of gg in λ\lambda and g​𝝈g\boldsymbol{\sigma} denotes the configuration transformed by gg. Starting from the parameters obtained in the initial optimization, we optimize |Ψλ⟩|\Psi_{\lambda}\rangle for a further 300300 steps at a fixed learning rate of 3×10−33\times 10^{-3}, with all other settings unchanged.
